newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: REBOUND IN EMPLOYMENT EXPECTED IN NEW FIGURES OUT TODAY
Figures out today are expected to show a strong rebound in employment in Australia, after the biggest monthly fall in three years.
Most analysts expect the number of people employed to have risen by by around 40,000 in June, correcting a similar decline in May.
This would leave average jobs growth at around 5,000 per month this year, a trend that is seen as flat.
Societe Generale Chief Economist, Glenn Maguire, said he does not expect much good news for the unemployment rate, which currently stands at 8.7 per cent.
He said things should have improved in June.
"The market is expecting a rebound of 40,000, which will correct that fall, and essentially leave annual jobs growth roughly unchanged over the last year".
"The pace of jobs growth at the moment is only enought to absorb new entrants into the workforce," he said.
Today's figures, plus forthcoming data on inflation and wages, are expected to be crucial to Reserve Bank calculations on interest rates.
MIXED UNION REACTION ON BLACK COAL INDUSTRY INQUIRY
There is mixed reaction from unions about the planned Industry Commission inquiry into the international competitiveness of the black coal industry.
The Construction Forestry Mining and Energy Union will meet with the Federal Government today to discuss the agenda of the inquiry.
The Government says the inquiry is necessary to test the productivity of the industry against export competitors.
But the CFMEU says the inquiry is being held at the prompting of resources giant Rio Tinto.
The union's Tony Maher, however, says he believes the inquiry may still have positive outcomes.
The United Mineworkers Federation says the Government has not asked for the Federation's input on the inquiry.
The union's Wayne McAndrew said he believes the inquiry could undermine conditions for mine workers.
VOLUNTARY EUTHANASIA BILL PASSES FIRST HURDLE IN SA
A private member's bill on voluntary euthanasia has passed a hurdle in the South Australian Parliament.
The Legislative Council has agreed to further debate the bill, after passing the second reading, in a 13 to 8 conscience vote.
The bill was put forward by Opposition MP Anne Levy, who said part of her motivation stems from the death of her husband, from cancer, more than 20 years ago.
"It's the first step along a long road but a very important step, and it's the furtherest that any bill on euthanasia has ever gone, other than the Northern Territory legislation." she said.
The Upper House also voted to set up a select committee to investigate the right-to-die issue.
Ms Levy said after it reports to Parliament, she would like to see an amendment to the bill ensuring it could not become law until there's a referendum that supports voluntary euthanasia.
Ms Levy's bill would have to be read, and voted on, on a third occassion, before going to the House of Assembly.
AUSTRALIA'S TREATMENT OF ACTIVIST MAKES NEWS IN EUROPE
The Federal Government's deportation of American black activist, Lorenzo Ervin, has made its way into newspapers in Europe.
Les Malezer, the head of Queensland aboriginal organisation, FAIRA, is in Brussels with an indigenous delegation and says the deportation has not helped Australia's reputation.
Mr Malezer says there is a large interest in Europe about social justice issues and this sort of action by the Federal Government is not going unnoticed around the world.
He said the only news about Australia in a newspaper he had read was reaction to the arrest of the former Black Panther.
"I believe that quite clearly, Europe at least as part of the rest of the world, have a perception that Australia is becoming very indifferent to human rights and to race issues", he said.
FAMILY COURT DECISION HAILED A VICTORY FOR CHILDREN
The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission has welcomed a landmark Family Court decision describing it as a "victory for children".
In Brisbane, the court dismissed an appeal by a man against a decision allowing his former wife to move interstate with their children.
Human Rights Commissioner, Chris Sidoti, says the central issue in such cases must be what's in the best interests of the child.

"These sorts of circumstances where the dispute goes to the court and has to be decided by the court is very much a second, third or fourth best way of looking at childrens' interests," Mr Sidoti said.

"The important thing then is to ensure that when that is necessary, when this kind of case does arise, that the children are placed at the centre of the court's determination. I'm pleased in this case the court has affirmed that principle," he said.
WIDER INVESTIGATIONS INTO VICTORIAN RELIGIOUS SECT
Police investigating the activities of a Victorian religious sect will widen their inquiries, to check the group's links overseas and interstate.
Three witnesses have contacted police with information about the so-called doomsday sect, The Order of Saint Charbel, which runs a commune at Tyaak, in central Victoria.
Police will investigate claims the group planned a mass suicide, has a stockpile of weapons, and that members were told to dig graves on the property.
Last week, a senior Catholic official told ABC Radio, members have built bunkers in case the Hale-Bopp comet crashes into the sun.
Police Chief Inspector, Ken Allen, has urged former members of the sect to come forward.

"There may still be others...who wish to come forward and I would urge them to do so, if indeed they feel they have any information that may assist us investigate breaches of the criminal law", he said.
WALLABY TEST SIDE SETTLED
Wallaby coach Greg Smith has settled on his starting fifteen for Saturday's rugby Test against England at the Sydney Football Stadium.
The side is Blades, Foley, McKenzie, Morgan, Eales, captain, Manu, Robinson, Coker, Gregan, Horan, Roff, Holbeck, Little, Tune and Burke.
David Wilson, originally bracketed in a backrow of four, is included in a reserves list along with Hardy, Larkham, Payne, Cockbain, Caputo and Andrew Blades, with one to be omitted.
